title: Source coding
text:
Definition 1 (Binary code) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable. A binary code for \(X\) assigns each value \(x\) a codeword, a finite string of binary digits, of length \(\ell(x)\).











Definition 2 (Uniquely decodable code) A binary code is uniquely decodable if every finite sequence of codewords, written one after another, can be split back into codewords in only one way.











Definition 3 (Expected length) The expected length of a binary code for \(X\), where \(X\) has probability mass function \(p(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{P}(X=x)\), is
\[L \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[\ell(X)\right]\mathclose{} = \sum_{x} p(x) \, \ell(x).\]











Remark 1 (Short codewords for common values). A code with a small expected length gives frequent values short codewords and rare values long ones, since each value’s length counts in \(L\) in proportion to its probability.

title: Source coding
text:
Definition 1 (Binary code) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable. A binary code for \(X\) assigns each value \(x\) a codeword, a finite string of binary digits, of length \(\ell(x)\).











Definition 2 (Uniquely decodable code) A binary code is uniquely decodable if every finite sequence of codewords, written one after another, can be split back into codewords in only one way.











Definition 3 (Expected length) The expected length of a binary code for \(X\), where \(X\) has probability mass function \(p(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{P}(X=x)\), is
\[L \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[\ell(X)\right]\mathclose{} = \sum_{x} p(x) \, \ell(x).\]











Remark 1 (Short codewords for common values). A code with a small expected length gives frequent values short codewords and rare values long ones, since each value’s length counts in \(L\) in proportion to its probability.

title: Source coding
text:
2 The source coding theorem








Theorem 1 (Source coding theorem) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable that takes finitely many values, at least two of them with positive probability, and let \(H_2(X)\) be its entropy with base-2 logarithms.

Every uniquely decodable binary code for \(X\) has expected length \(L \ge H_2(X)\).
Some uniquely decodable binary code for \(X\) has expected length \(L < H_2(X) + 1\).
Coding blocks of \(n\) independent copies of \(X\) at a time, some uniquely decodable binary code spends, on average, fewer than \(H_2(X) + 1/n\) binary digits per copy.












Remark 2 (Where the theorem comes from). Shannon (1948) proved that entropy is the limit on how far the output of a source can be compressed. Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 5.3 to 5.5) prove each part of Theorem 1. For part 2, they give each value \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\) the length \(\ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil\), its surprisal in bits rounded up; the Kraft inequality (Cover and Thomas 2006, sec. 5.2) guarantees that a code with these lengths exists.

title: Source coding
text:
3 Coding with the wrong distribution








Theorem 2 (The cost of coding with the wrong distribution) Let \(X\) take finitely many values, with probability mass function \(p\), and let \(q\) be a probability mass function, possibly different from \(p\), with \(q(x) > 0\) wherever \(p(x) > 0\). Suppose a code gives each value \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\) the length \(\ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2 q(x) \rceil\). Then its expected length \(L\) under \(p\) satisfies
\[H_2(p, q) \le L < H_2(p, q) + 1,\]
where \(H_2(p, q)\) is the cross-entropy of \(q\) relative to \(p\), with base-2 logarithms.










ProofProof






Proof. Every sum here runs over the values \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\). Rounding up adds less than one binary digit, so for each such \(x\)
\[-\log_2 q(x) \le \ell(x) < -\log_2 q(x) + 1.\]
Multiply each part by \(p(x) > 0\) and sum. Since \(\sum_{x} p(x) = 1\),
\[
-\sum_{x} p(x) \log_2 q(x)
\le \sum_{x} p(x) \, \ell(x)
< -\sum_{x} p(x) \log_2 q(x) + 1.
\]
The middle sum is \(L\), and the outer sums are \(H_2(p, q)\).











Remark 3 (Cross-entropy is the cost of the wrong code). Write \(H_2(p)\) for the entropy of a random variable with mass function \(p\), and \(D_2(p \,\|\, q)\) for the Kullback–Leibler divergence of \(q\) from \(p\), both with base-2 logarithms. Cross-entropy splits into those two parts:
\[H_2(p, q) = H_2(p) + D_2(p \,\|\, q).\]
By Theorem 1, no uniquely decodable code averages fewer than \(H_2(p)\) bits. By Theorem 2, a code built for \(q\) costs about \(D_2(p \,\|\, q)\) bits per value more than that. The divergence is never negative, and it is \(0\) only when \(q = p\) (Cover and Thomas 2006, sec. 2.6), so the excess vanishes only when the code was built for the true distribution. Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 5.4) state Theorem 2 in this form, with \(H_2(p) + D_2(p \,\|\, q)\) in place of \(H_2(p, q)\).











Remark 4 (Why models are fit by minimizing cross-entropy). Fitting a classifier by minimizing cross-entropy chooses the model’s distribution \(q\) so that a code built for \(q\) would spend as few bits as possible on the observed labels. By Remark 3, that pushes \(q\) toward the distribution the labels came from.
For a single labeled example, let \(e\) be the distribution that puts all its mass on the observed label. Then \(H_2(e) = 0\) (as for a coin that always lands heads), so the example’s cross-entropy loss \(H_2(e, q)\) equals \(D_2(e \,\|\, q)\): every bit the loss reports is a wasted one.

text:

Cover, Thomas M., and Joy A. Thomas. 2006. Elements of Information Theory. 2nd ed. Wiley-Interscience. https://doi.org/10.1002/047174882X.

title: Entropy and mutual information
text: This page builds on the definitions of entropy, cross-entropy and Kullback–Leibler divergence in Probability for Data Science.

title: Entropy and mutual information
text:
1 Surprisal








Definition 1 (Surprisal) The surprisal of an outcome \(x\) of a discrete random variable \(X\) with \(\operatorname{P}(X=x) > 0\) is
\[s(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}-\log \operatorname{P}(X=x).\]
With base-2 logarithms, surprisal is measured in bits; with natural logarithms, in nats.











Example 1 (Counting bits with fair coins) One toss of a fair coin has \(2\) equally likely outcomes, and one binary digit is enough to record which one happened. Two tosses have \(4\) outcomes, and two binary digits record them. In general, \(k\) tosses have \(n = 2^k\) equally likely outcomes, and \(k = \log_2 n\) binary digits record them.
Each of those \(n\) outcomes has probability \(p = 1/n\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
k
&= \log_2 n \\
&= \log_2 \frac{1}{p} \\
&= -\log_2 p,
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the surprisal of the outcome, in bits.
Ten tosses that all land heads have probability \(2^{-10}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(\text{ten heads})
&= -\log_2 2^{-10} \\
&= 10 \text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]











Remark 1 (Unlikely outcomes carry more information). Surprisal is large when an outcome was unlikely, and it falls to \(0\) as the outcome becomes certain. Correctly predicting heads on one toss of a fair coin is worth \(1\) bit; correctly predicting ten heads in a row is worth \(10\) bits. MacKay (2003, sec. 2.4) calls \(s(x)\) in bits the Shannon information content of the outcome \(x\).











Remark 2 (Entropy is expected surprisal). The entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) is the expectation of its surprisal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X)
&= \operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[-\log \operatorname{P}(X)\right]\mathclose{} \\
&= \operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[s(X)\right]\mathclose{}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(H(X)\) is the average number of bits (with base-2 logarithms) needed to record an outcome of \(X\) when each outcome \(x\) costs \(s(x)\) bits. The source coding theorem, on a later page of these notes, makes that average precise: no uniquely decodable code does better.

title: Entropy and mutual information
text:
2 Joint and conditional entropy








Definition 2 (Joint entropy) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be discrete random variables with joint probability mass function \(p(x, y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{P}(X=x, Y=y)\). Their joint entropy is the entropy of the pair \((X, Y)\):
\[H(X, Y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}-\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(x, y),\]
where the sum runs over the pairs with \(p(x, y) > 0\).











Definition 3 (Entropy given one value) For \(X\) and \(Y\) as in Definition 2, write \(p(y \mid x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{P}(Y=y \mid X=x)\). The entropy of \(Y\) given \(X=x\), for a value \(x\) with \(\operatorname{P}(X=x) > 0\), is
\[H(Y \mid X=x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}-\sum_{y} p(y \mid x) \log p(y \mid x),\]
where the sum runs over the values \(y\) with \(p(y \mid x) > 0\).











Definition 4 (Conditional entropy) For \(X\) and \(Y\) as in Definition 2, write \(p(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{P}(X=x)\). The conditional entropy of \(Y\) given \(X\) averages the entropy of \(Y\) given each value of \(X\) over the distribution of \(X\):
\[H(Y \mid X) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{x} p(x) \, H(Y \mid X=x),\]
where the sum runs over the values \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\).











Theorem 1 (Chain rule for entropy) For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\),
\[H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X).\]










ProofProof






Proof. Use the notation of Definition 3 and Definition 4, with every sum over the pairs with \(p(x, y) > 0\). Since \(p(x, y) = p(x) \, p(y \mid x)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X, Y)
&= -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(x, y) \\
&= -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log \mathopen{}\left[p(x) \, p(y \mid x)\right]\mathclose{} \\
&= -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(x)
   - \sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(y \mid x) \\
&= -\sum_{x} \log p(x) \sum_{y} p(x, y)
   - \sum_{x} p(x) \sum_{y} p(y \mid x) \log p(y \mid x) \\
&= -\sum_{x} p(x) \log p(x)
   + \sum_{x} p(x) \, H(Y \mid X=x) \\
&= H(X) + H(Y \mid X).
\end{aligned}
\]
The fourth line groups the terms by \(x\) and uses \(p(x, y) = p(x) \, p(y \mid x)\) in the second sum; the fifth uses \(\sum_{y} p(x, y) = p(x)\) and the definition of \(H(Y \mid X=x)\).

title: Entropy and mutual information
text:
3 Mutual information








Definition 5 (Mutual information) The mutual information between discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with finite entropies is the reduction in the entropy of \(Y\) from learning \(X\):
\[I(X; Y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}H(Y) - H(Y \mid X),\]
where \(H(Y \mid X)\) is the conditional entropy.











Theorem 2 (Mutual information is symmetric) For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with finite entropies,
\[I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = I(Y; X).\]










ProofProof






Proof. The chain rule expands \(H(X, Y)\) in either order:
\[H(X) + H(Y \mid X) = H(X, Y) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y).\]
Subtracting \(H(X \mid Y) + H(Y \mid X)\) from the outer two expressions gives
\[H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X).\]
The right side is \(I(X; Y)\) by Definition 5, and the left side is \(I(Y; X)\) by the same definition.











Remark 3 (Mutual information as a divergence). Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 2.3) define mutual information as the Kullback–Leibler divergence of the joint distribution of \((X, Y)\) from the product of its marginals, and show that this equals \(H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\) (Cover and Thomas 2006, sec. 2.4). Since a Kullback–Leibler divergence is never negative, and is \(0\) only when the two distributions are equal (Cover and Thomas 2006, sec. 2.6), \(I(X; Y) \ge 0\), with equality exactly when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. Learning \(X\) never raises the entropy of \(Y\) on average.











Definition 6 (Information gain) A decision tree splits the points at a node into branches. The information gain of the split is the entropy of the class labels at the node, minus the entropy of the labels in each branch, weighted by the share of the node’s points that branch holds (Quinlan 1986).











Remark 4 (Information gain is mutual information). Draw one point uniformly at random from the node of Definition 6, and let \(Y\) be its class and \(X\) the branch it falls into. Then the entropy at the node is \(H(Y)\), the weighted entropy left in the branches is \(H(Y \mid X)\), and the information gain is the mutual information \(I(X; Y)\).











Exercise 1 (Choosing between two splits) A node holds \(20\) points, \(10\) red and \(10\) green. Two candidate splits each send the points into two branches:



split
branch
red
green




A
yes
\(4\)
\(0\)

Draw one point uniformly at random from the node, let \(Y\) be its color, and let \(X\) be the branch it falls into (Remark 4). The information gain of each split (Definition 6) is then \(I(X; Y)\). Use base-2 logarithms throughout.

Compute \(H(Y)\).
For each split, compute \(H(Y \mid X = x)\) for both branches, and then \(H(Y \mid X)\).
Compute the information gain \(I(X; Y)\) for each split. Which split has the larger gain?











SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 

Half the points are red, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y)
&= -\tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} \\
&= 1 \text{ bit}.
\end{aligned}
\]
A branch holding one color only has entropy \(0\). For split A, the “no” branch holds \(6\) red and \(10\) green points of \(16\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y \mid X = \text{no})
&= -\tfrac{6}{16} \log_2 \tfrac{6}{16} - \tfrac{10}{16} \log_2 \tfrac{10}{16} \\
&\approx 0.531 + 0.424 \\
&\approx 0.954 \text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The “yes” branch holds \(4\) of the \(20\) points and the “no” branch \(16\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y \mid X)
&= \tfrac{4}{20} \cdot 0 + \tfrac{16}{20} \cdot 0.954 \\
&\approx 0.764 \text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For split B, the “yes” branch holds \(5\) red and \(10\) green points of \(15\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y \mid X = \text{yes})
&= -\tfrac{1}{3} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{3} - \tfrac{2}{3} \log_2 \tfrac{2}{3} \\
&\approx 0.528 + 0.390 \\
&\approx 0.918 \text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The “yes” branch holds \(15\) of the \(20\) points and the “no” branch \(5\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y \mid X)
&= \tfrac{15}{20} \cdot 0.918 + \tfrac{5}{20} \cdot 0 \\
&\approx 0.689 \text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By Definition 5, the gain is \(H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\):

split A: \(1 - 0.764 = 0.236\) bits
split B: \(1 - 0.689 = 0.311\) bits

Split B has the larger gain. Both splits isolate a branch of one color, so the gain depends on the other, mixed branch. B’s mixed branch, \(5\) red against \(10\) green, is more lopsided than A’s \(6\) against \(10\), so it has less entropy, and it also holds fewer of the points, \(15\) against \(16\), so its entropy gets less weight.

title: Channel capacity
text: A channel carries symbols from a sender to a receiver, and noise corrupts some of them. This page measures how much information a channel can carry, using the mutual information between what goes in and what comes out.

title: Channel capacity
text:
1 Channels








Definition 1 (Discrete memoryless channel) A discrete channel has a finite input alphabet \(\mathcal{X}\), a finite output alphabet \(\mathcal{Y}\), and, for each input \(x \in \mathcal{X}\), a probability mass function \(p(y \mid x)\) on \(\mathcal{Y}\): the probability that the channel outputs \(y\) when it is sent \(x\). The channel is memoryless if, over \(n\) uses, each output depends only on the input sent at that use:
\[
\operatorname{P}(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_n = y_n \mid X_1 = x_1, \dots, X_n = x_n)
= \prod_{i=1}^{n} p(y_i \mid x_i).
\]
This is the setup of Cover and Thomas (2006, chap. 7).











Definition 2 (Binary symmetric channel) The binary symmetric channel with crossover probability \(\epsilon \in [0, 1]\) is the discrete memoryless channel with \(\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{Y} = \{0, 1\}\) that flips its input with probability \(\epsilon\):
\[
p(y \mid x) =
\begin{cases}
1 - \epsilon & \text{if } y = x, \\
\epsilon & \text{if } y \ne x.
\end{cases}
\]











Definition 3 (Binary erasure channel) The binary erasure channel with erasure probability \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\) is the discrete memoryless channel with \(\mathcal{X} = \{0, 1\}\) and \(\mathcal{Y} = \{0, \mathrm{e}, 1\}\) that delivers its input with probability \(1 - \alpha\) and otherwise outputs the erasure symbol \(\mathrm{e}\):
\[
p(y \mid x) =
\begin{cases}
1 - \alpha & \text{if } y = x, \\
\alpha & \text{if } y = \mathrm{e}, \\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]











Remark 1 (Erasures are visible). On the binary erasure channel the receiver knows which symbols were lost, but not what they were. On the binary symmetric channel the receiver cannot tell which symbols were flipped.

title: Channel capacity
text:
2 Capacity








Definition 4 (Channel capacity) Send one input \(X\) through a discrete memoryless channel, and let \(Y\) be the output. The joint distribution of \((X, Y)\) is \(\operatorname{P}(X = x, Y = y) = \operatorname{P}(X = x) \, p(y \mid x)\), so the mutual information \(I(X; Y)\) depends on the channel and on the input distribution. The capacity of the channel is the largest mutual information any input distribution achieves:
\[C \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\max_{\operatorname{P}(X = \cdot)} I(X; Y),\]
where the maximum runs over all probability mass functions on \(\mathcal{X}\) (Cover and Thomas 2006, chap. 7). With base-2 logarithms, \(C\) is measured in bits per channel use.











Remark 2 (What capacity measures). \(I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y)\) (symmetry of mutual information) is the uncertainty about the input, minus the uncertainty about the input left after seeing the output. So \(I(X; Y)\) is how much one output tells the receiver about the input, on average, and the capacity is that amount when the sender chooses how often to send each input as well as possible.











Definition 5 (Binary entropy function) The binary entropy function is
\[h(\epsilon) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}-\epsilon \log_2 \epsilon - (1 - \epsilon) \log_2 (1 - \epsilon)\]
for \(0 < \epsilon < 1\), with \(h(0) = h(1) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}0\).











Remark 3 (Binary entropy is the entropy of a coin). \(h(\epsilon)\) is the entropy, in bits, of a random variable that takes one of two values, one of them with probability \(\epsilon\). It is \(0\) when the outcome is certain and largest, \(1\) bit, at \(\epsilon = 1/2\).











Theorem 1 (Capacity of the binary symmetric channel) The binary symmetric channel with crossover probability \(\epsilon\) has capacity
\[C = 1 - h(\epsilon) \text{ bits per channel use},\]
where \(h\) is the binary entropy function. A uniformly distributed input achieves it.










ProofProof






Proof. Fix any input distribution. By the definition of mutual information,
\[I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X).\]
Given \(X = x\), the output equals \(x\) with probability \(1 - \epsilon\) and differs from it with probability \(\epsilon\), so the entropy of \(Y\) given \(X = x\) is \(h(\epsilon)\) for both inputs. Averaging over \(x\), the conditional entropy is \(H(Y \mid X) = h(\epsilon)\), whatever the input distribution.
\(Y\) takes two values, so \(H(Y) \le \log_2 2 = 1\) bit (Cover and Thomas 2006, sec. 2.6). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(X; Y)
&= H(Y) - h(\epsilon) \\
&\le 1 - h(\epsilon).
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0, 1\}\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{P}(Y = 1)
&= \operatorname{P}(X = 0) \, \epsilon + \operatorname{P}(X = 1) \, (1 - \epsilon) \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \epsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} (1 - \epsilon) \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2},
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(H(Y) = 1\) bit and \(I(X; Y) = 1 - h(\epsilon)\). The bound is attained, so it is the maximum \(C\).











Example 1 (A channel that flips one bit in ten) For a binary symmetric channel with \(\epsilon = 0.1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
h(0.1)
&= -0.1 \log_2 0.1 - 0.9 \log_2 0.9 \\
&\approx 0.332 + 0.137 \\
&\approx 0.469 \text{ bits},
\end{aligned}
\]
so by Theorem 1 the capacity is
\[C \approx 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 \text{ bits per channel use}.\]
Each use carries one binary digit, but on average only about half a bit of it gets through. At \(\epsilon = 1/2\), \(h(1/2) = 1\) and \(C = 0\): the output is independent of the input. At \(\epsilon = 1\), \(C = 1\) again, since the receiver can flip every bit back.











Exercise 1 (Capacity of the binary erasure channel) Send \(X\) through the binary erasure channel with erasure probability \(\alpha\), where \(0 < \alpha < 1\), and write \(\pi \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{P}(X = 1)\). Let \(E\) be \(1\) if the output \(Y\) is the erasure symbol \(\mathrm{e}\), and \(0\) otherwise. Use base-2 logarithms and the binary entropy function \(h\).

Show that \(H(Y \mid X) = h(\alpha)\).
\(E\) is a function of \(Y\). Use the chain rule for entropy, expanded in both orders, to show that \(H(Y) = H(E) + H(Y \mid E)\).
Show that \(H(Y) = h(\alpha) + (1 - \alpha) \, h(\pi)\).
Conclude that the capacity is \(C = 1 - \alpha\) bits per channel use.











SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 

Given \(X = x\), the output is \(x\) with probability \(1 - \alpha\) and \(\mathrm{e}\) with probability \(\alpha\), so \(H(Y \mid X = x) = h(\alpha)\) for both inputs, and averaging over \(x\) gives \(H(Y \mid X) = h(\alpha)\).
The chain rule gives
\[H(Y) + H(E \mid Y) = H(Y, E) = H(E) + H(Y \mid E).\]
Each value \(y\) of \(Y\) fixes \(E\), so \(H(E \mid Y = y) = 0\) for every \(y\), and \(H(E \mid Y) = 0\). Hence \(H(Y) = H(E) + H(Y \mid E)\).
The channel erases with probability \(\alpha\) whatever the input, so \(E\) is independent of \(X\) and \(H(E) = h(\alpha)\). Given \(E = 1\), \(Y = \mathrm{e}\) for certain, so \(H(Y \mid E = 1) = 0\). Given \(E = 0\), \(Y = X\), and since \(E\) is independent of \(X\), \(\operatorname{P}(Y = 1 \mid E = 0) = \operatorname{P}(X = 1) = \pi\), so \(H(Y \mid E = 0) = h(\pi)\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y)
&= H(E) + \operatorname{P}(E = 1) \, H(Y \mid E = 1) + \operatorname{P}(E = 0) \, H(Y \mid E = 0) \\
&= h(\alpha) + \alpha \cdot 0 + (1 - \alpha) \, h(\pi) \\
&= h(\alpha) + (1 - \alpha) \, h(\pi).
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining parts 1 and 3,
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(X; Y)
&= H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) \\
&= h(\alpha) + (1 - \alpha) \, h(\pi) - h(\alpha) \\
&= (1 - \alpha) \, h(\pi).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(h(\pi) \le 1\), with equality at \(\pi = 1/2\), the maximum over input distributions is \(C = 1 - \alpha\). The receiver loses a fraction \(\alpha\) of the bits and learns the rest exactly; Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 7.1) reach the same capacity.

title: Channel capacity
text:
3 The noisy-channel coding theorem








Definition 6 (Channel code and rate) An \((M, n)\) channel code for a discrete memoryless channel sends one of \(M\) messages, \(w \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), in \(n\) uses of the channel. It has

an encoder, which maps each message \(w\) to a codeword \((x_1(w), \dots, x_n(w))\) of \(n\) inputs, and
a decoder, which maps each sequence of \(n\) outputs to a guess at \(w\).

Its rate is
\[R \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\log_2 M}{n} \text{ bits per channel use},\]
and its maximal probability of error \(\lambda^{(n)}\) is the largest, over messages \(w\), of the probability that the decoder’s guess is wrong when \(w\) is sent. These are the definitions of Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 7.5).











Example 2 (Sending each bit three times) To send one bit over the binary symmetric channel with \(\epsilon = 0.1\), send it three times and decode by majority vote. This is a \((2, 3)\) channel code, with rate \(R = 1/3\). The decoder is wrong when two or three of the copies are flipped, which happens with probability
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda^{(3)}
&= 3 \epsilon^2 (1 - \epsilon) + \epsilon^3 \\
&= 3 (0.01)(0.9) + 0.001 \\
&= 0.028,
\end{aligned}
\]
down from \(0.1\) for sending the bit once. Repeating more often lowers the error further, but the rate falls toward \(0\) as it does. MacKay (2003, chap. 1) works through this code.











Theorem 2 (Noisy-channel coding theorem) Let \(C\) be the capacity of a discrete memoryless channel.

For every rate \(R < C\) there is a sequence of \((\lceil 2^{nR} \rceil, n)\) channel codes, for \(n = 1, 2, \dots\), whose maximal probability of error \(\lambda^{(n)}\) tends to \(0\).
Conversely, any sequence of \((\lceil 2^{nR} \rceil, n)\) codes with \(\lambda^{(n)} \to 0\) has \(R \le C\).












Remark 4 (Reliable communication at a positive rate). Example 2 buys a lower error rate with a lower rate, and repetition alone drives the error to \(0\) only as the rate falls to \(0\). Theorem 2 says that this trade-off is not forced: over the channel of Example 1, long enough codes send about \(0.53\) bits per channel use with an error probability as small as we like. Above capacity, no code can.
Shannon (1948) stated the theorem and sketched its proof. Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 7.7) prove part 1 by choosing codewords at random, and Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 7.9) prove part 2 with Fano’s inequality. MacKay (2003, chap. 9 and 10) gives another account.

title: Information Theory for Data Science
text:
Information theory measures uncertainty and information: how many bits a message needs, how much one random variable tells us about another, and how fast data can cross a noisy channel. Data science uses its quantities directly: cross-entropy is the loss in logistic regression and neural networks, Kullback–Leibler divergence links maximum likelihood to model fit, and mutual information drives the information gain of decision trees.
These notes collect the information theory that data science courses use. They are new. The pages written so far are:

Entropy and mutual information: surprisal, joint and conditional entropy, mutual information, and the information gain of decision trees
Source coding: the source coding theorem, and cross-entropy as the cost of coding with the wrong distribution
Channel capacity: discrete memoryless channels, the capacity of the binary symmetric and erasure channels, and the noisy-channel coding theorem

The planned topics still to come are:

Kullback–Leibler divergence and its link to maximum likelihood
Huffman and arithmetic codes
proofs of the noisy-channel coding theorem, and codes that approach capacity
Kolmogorov complexity, and how it relates to Shannon entropy

Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence are defined in Probability for Data Science; pages here link to those definitions rather than repeating them. Computational complexity has its own library, Computational Complexity for Data Science.

title: Information Theory for Data Science
section: Where to read about the planned topics
text:
Where to read about the planned topics
Stanford’s information theory courses cover many of the planned topics above, and they publish their course pages:

EE 276, Information Theory (Tsachy Weissman) covers entropy and mutual information, the asymptotic equipartition property, prefix codes and Huffman codes, channel capacity and the channel coding theorem, and rate distortion. Its reading page lists books and Shannon’s papers.
EE 274, Data Compression, Theory and Applications covers entropy coding and how tools such as gzip and bzip2 work, then lossy image and video coding.

The courses’ own notes and slides carry no license, so these notes link to them and do not reuse their text.

title: Information Theory for Data Science
section: Using these notes in another site
text:
Using these notes in another site
Course sites link to these pages by URL; they do not include this repository as a git submodule. A host site that keeps a copy of this repository at its root, named ids, can still include fragments with paths that start with ids/. This site includes its own fragments the same way, through a ids symlink that points at the repository root.
Quarto resolves @id cross-references only within one rendered page, so a host site that links to a result here uses an explicit link to the page and anchor.
